claims.text: SPS-processed TiVNbTa has a single-phase BCC dendritic structure.
TiVNbTa has a yield strength of 330 MPa at 1273 K.
TiVNbTa has a compressive strength of 423 MPa at 1273 K under 30% strain.
A controlled carbon addition will be introduced during SPS of mechanically alloyed TiVNbTa powder.
Introducing carbon during SPS of TiVNbTa will induce in situ TiC precipitation.
The induced TiC precipitates will be nanometer-scale and uniformly dispersed in the BCC matrix.
Adjusting carbon content can promote nanoprecipitation without excessive carbide coarsening.
A processing range of approximately 1200–1400 °C is typical for SPS fabrication of TiVNbTa.
TiC nanoparticles will impede dislocation motion at high temperature and provide dispersion strengthening.
Carbon-modified TiVNbTa will have increased yield strength at 1273 K relative to the 330 MPa baseline.
Carbon-modified TiVNbTa will have increased compressive strength at 1273 K relative to the 423 MPa baseline.
The strength improvement will occur under approximately 30% strain loading.
The TiC reinforcement will not substantially reduce the alloy's ductility.
The TiC reinforcement will not substantially reduce the thermal conductivity required for heat transfer between W and CuCrZr.
The modification will not compromise lower-temperature properties needed for thermal transfer across the W–CuCrZr interface.
Carbon diffusion during SPS can form refractory-metal carbides in an HEA.
The optimal carbon content and precise high-temperature strength improvement remain uncertain.

contradictions.description: The baseline compressive strength is 423 MPa, but the prediction and falsification rule use 330 MPa as a threshold for both yield and compressive strength. A compressive strength above 330 MPa could still be below the 423 MPa baseline and therefore would not constitute the claimed improvement.

The hypothesis separately predicts TiC formation and improved strength, but the falsification rule requires both absence of fine TiC and absence of strength improvement. Failure of either individual prediction alone would not trigger falsification under this conjunctive rule.
